limitations: One task row, two callers, two receipt identities and at most two attempts per caller.
Standard scheduled-to-fired claims are covered. Follow-up claim expectations, recurrence, host admission policy, apply-intent reservation and general lifecycle verbs still need separate models.
The model represents exact state/metadata/definition equality using a revision token and atomic SQL statements. SQL execution and JSON projection need the implementation tests.
One daily recurring task over three occurrences; the owner acts at most once between two ticks, on a scheduled or fired row.
The replay covers cron and during_window triggers with in-memory stores; interval triggers, applyWithResult and a snoozed row are separate tests in runner-pending-occurrence.test.ts.
Reopen, gate denials and the global pause keep their existing coverage; the SQL stores persist the same row fields.

Progress through the three occurrences requires weak fairness of each enabled tick and settlement of tick and owner-verb work. Paused clocks have an explicit no-fairness counterexample. No wall-clock bound or external delivery success is proved.
One deferred first-wins registration, one shared task and two callers.
Work already started retains its dispatcher; the shared store claim is not reset. Real SQL behavior is checked by the implementation case.
Bounded safety only. Completion requires fair execution of an accepted operation; network/provider liveness and hot unregistration are outside this model.

One runtime, two worker generations, one deferred hook per generation and one canonical driver row. Real runtime and file-backed SQLite cases hold the first insert across unload, verify cleanup and fresh reload after acknowledged and unacknowledged commits, and resume an obsolete seed callback after reload.

Progress requires fair database and teardown settlement. A failed cleanup can retain the canonical row for later reconciliation. Running worker effects, multiple runtimes, legacy duplicate rows, consumer-host takeover and unbounded progress remain outside the model.
Two owner-reply scans, one fired task with a passing completion check and one pipeline.onComplete child.
A commit writes the row, the completed log row and the child in one step; partial failures inside settleTerminal keep their existing coverage.

Other verbs between a scan's read and its commit are covered by runner-completion-settle.test.ts (a snooze, no mutation policy) and runner-host-admission.integration.test.ts (an owner disable under the host policy); the SQL store's conditional write by the store tests, not by this model.

Scan progress requires weak fairness of each enabled read and commit and settlement of the owner and store calls. No wall-clock bound or permanent store failure recovery is proved; the no-fairness progress claim must have a temporal loop counterexample.
